content: The Black Death, also known as the Black Plague, was one of the most devastating pandemics in human history. It is widely believed to have been caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which is associated with bubonic plague, although some researchers have recently suggested other possible causes. The pandemic is thought to have originated in Central Asia or India and spread to Europe in the 1340s. Globally, it is estimated to have caused the deaths of approximately 75 million people, with 25 to 50 million of those deaths occurring in Europe. The Black Death is believed to have killed between 30% and 60% of Europe’s population, reducing the world’s population from an estimated 450 million to between 350 and 375 million by the year 1400. The bubonic plague is thought to have recurred in Europe every generation with varying levels of virulence and mortality until the 1700s. Over this period, more than 100 plague epidemics swept across Europe. For example, in 1603, the plague killed 38,000 Londoners. Other significant outbreaks during the 17th century included the Italian Plague of 1629–1631, the Great Plague of Seville (1647–1652), the Great Plague of London (1665–1666), and the Great Plague of Vienna (1679). After the Great Plague of Marseille (1720–1722), the Great Plague of 1738 in Eastern Europe, and the 1771 plague in Moscow, the disease appears to have disappeared from Europe by the 19th century. The 14th-century outbreak of the Black Death had profound effects on Europe’s population and social structure. It dealt a severe blow to the Roman Catholic Church and led to widespread persecution of minorities, including Jews, foreigners, beggars, and lepers. The uncertainty of survival created a pervasive mood of morbidity, influencing people to adopt a live for the moment attitude, as depicted by Giovanni Boccaccio in The Decameron (1353). Medieval people referred to the catastrophe as the Great Pestilence or the Great Plague, while contemporary writers called it the Great Mortality. The term Black Death was first introduced in 1833. It is popularly thought that the name derived from the striking late-stage symptoms of the disease, such as blackened skin due to subepidermal hemorrhages (purpura) and gangrene (acral necrosis). However, the term more likely refers to the grim and dreadful nature of the event. The Black Death was characterized by the appearance of buboes (swollen lymph nodes) in the groin, neck, and armpits, similar to the late 19th-century Asian bubonic plague. Early 20th-century scientists and historians assumed that the Black Death was caused by Yersinia pestis and spread by fleas, with the black rat (Rattus rattus) serving as a key vector. However, this view has been questioned in recent years. Some researchers suggest that the Black Death may still lie dormant, while others propose alternative explanations for its epidemiology. The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis is enzootic (commonly present) in populations of ground rodents in Central Asia. The most widely accepted theory places the first cases of the 14th-century pandemic in the steppes of Central Asia, although some speculate that it originated in northern India or Africa. From Central Asia, the disease spread east and west along the Silk Road, carried by Mongol armies and traders who benefited from the Pax Mongolica. The plague was reportedly introduced to Europe at the trading city of Caffa in Crimea in 1347. During a siege, the Mongol army, suffering from the disease, catapulted infected corpses over the city walls to infect the inhabitants. Genoese traders fleeing Caffa brought the plague by ship to Sicily and southern Europe, from where it spread further. The spread of the Black Death was exacerbated by pre-existing conditions such as war, famine, and climate changes. In China, the 13th-century Mongol conquests disrupted farming and trade, leading to widespread famine and a population decline from approximately 120 million to 60 million. In Europe, the end of the Medieval Warm Period brought harsher winters and reduced harvests. The Great Famine of 1315–1317, caused by population growth outstripping agricultural productivity, weakened immune systems and increased vulnerability to disease. Food shortages, skyrocketing prices, and malnutrition were widespread, creating a vicious cycle of hunger and disease. The Black Death spread rapidly through Europe, first striking port cities and then following trade routes by sea and land. The most common form of the disease during the pandemic was bubonic plague, which had a mortality rate of 30–75%. Symptoms included fever, headaches, painful swollen lymph nodes (buboes), nausea, vomiting, and general malaise. Most victims died within four to seven days of infection. Pneumonic plague, the second most common form, had a mortality rate of 90–95% and presented with fever, cough, and blood-tinged sputum. Septicemic plague, the least common form, was almost universally fatal and caused high fevers and purpura due to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The Black Death’s rapid spread and high mortality rate have led some researchers to question whether it was caused solely by Yersinia pestis. For example, the disease killed between half and two-thirds of Iceland’s population, despite the absence of rats on the island at the time. Some studies have found molecular evidence of Y. pestis in plague victims’ remains, while others have not. Alternative theories suggest that the Black Death may have been caused by other pathogens, such as pulmonary anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) or an Ebola-like virus. These theories are supported by differences in symptoms, seasonality, and patterns of recurrence compared to modern bubonic plague. Despite these debates, many historians and scientists maintain that the Black Death was caused by Yersinia pestis. They argue that the rapid spread of the disease could be explained by respiratory droplet transmission and low immunity levels in the European population. Archaeological evidence confirms the presence of black rats in medieval Europe, and DNA from Y. pestis has been identified in the remains of plague victims. The Black Death’s eventual decline in the 18th century may have been influenced by changes in rat ecology, human immunity, and other factors.
